pages.title: About — AJ Wiebe
pages.description: Researcher, then developer, then technical leader, then researcher again — the thread connecting AJ Wiebe’s career.
pages.text: About — AJ Wiebe – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About I write software, lead the people who write it, and study why ontologies and knowledge representation still matter to both. Researcher I started in research, not industry. At the University of Regina I worked on industrial applications of AI — ontologies, knowledge engineering, software generated from a formal model of a problem and a formal model of the software meant to solve it. That became my thesis, Ontology Driven Software Engineering Generator , and two conference papers along the way. Before the thesis: early jobs at SaskTel and the Canadian federal government, building geospatial tools and rich internet applications. Less relevant to what I do now, but it's where I learned to actually ship something. Developer After the thesis, I spent over a decade writing software client-side — iQmetrix and HP Enterprise Services first, then eight years at Solvera Solutions, where I went from developer to team lead to a seat on the Application Development Council, interviewing the next generation of developers. The scope kept expanding. First my own code. Then reviewing someone else's. Then setting the direction a whole team built in. Technical Leader Since 2022 I've led Bitovi's engagement with a Fortune 500 financial services company — architecture, staffing, delivery, and technical leadership across the account. I started as its only consultant. I still write code. Architecture stopped being a technical question and became an organizational one: how do you get developers you'll never personally meet to build things the same way. Researcher, Again Modern AI reopened the questions I started with. Neurosymbolic AI, knowledge graphs, AI agents — these are the same problems from my thesis, with better tools than I had in 2016. I'm not affiliated with a university. This is independent research, done the way I do everything else: build something, see what breaks, write it down. See Research for what that looks like right now, and Projects for what I'm building alongside it. A shorter public career summary can be found on LinkedIn . by AJ click to skip by AJ © AJ Wiebe source on github

pages.title: AI Briefing — AJ Wiebe
pages.description: Twitter/X, filtered down to what actually matters, delivered to Telegram twice a day.
pages.text: AI Briefing — AJ Wiebe – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Projects / AI Briefing AI Briefing Twitter/X, filtered down to what actually matters, delivered to Telegram twice a day. Why I was spending more time scrolling than learning. I wanted a system that reads everything so I don't have to, and only surfaces what's worth acting on. How it works Curated X lists feed through RSSHub, get deduplicated semantically, then get classified by Claude CLI into four buckets — act now, queue, inform, skip — weighted by a rolling 30-day credibility score per source. A weekly agent maps connections between the notes I save. Runs locally: Python, Redis, SQLite, Docker. What I learned Four categories was the right number. Three collapses "important" into "urgent." Five is more than I'll ever triage consistently. Code github.com/alexanderwiebe/ai-briefing by AJ click to skip by AJ © AJ Wiebe source on github

pages.title: aj-starter-gold — AJ Wiebe
pages.description: A type-safe, isomorphic TypeScript starter combining Angular and NestJS into one three-tier architecture.
pages.text: aj-starter-gold — AJ Wiebe – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Projects / aj-starter-gold aj-starter-gold A type-safe, isomorphic TypeScript starter combining Angular and NestJS into one three-tier architecture. Why I wanted a working reference for combining Angular and NestJS into a single three-tier system that shares real types across the client and server, instead of maintaining the same model twice in two languages or two disconnected TypeScript codebases. How it works Angular on the frontend, NestJS on the backend, both TypeScript, with a shared type layer between them so a model change is a compiler error on both ends, not a runtime surprise on one. What I learned The hard part isn't the code, it's the configuration — getting the build tooling, module boundaries, and shared types to agree so the two halves behave like one system instead of two projects glued together. pages.text: Research Knowledge Graph — AJ Wiebe – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Projects / Research Knowledge Graph Research Knowledge Graph A personal, plugin-first knowledge graph for academic research — not owned by any single vendor. Why Every research tool I've used — reference managers, note apps, AI assistants — wants to own the graph. I wanted the graph to outlast all of them. How it works The core defines capability contracts — a Research Library Connector, a Knowledge Store, a Scholarly Metadata Provider — and never talks to a specific product. Plugins implement the contracts. Swap a vendor, keep the graph. What I learned Still in design — nothing shipped yet. The hard part isn't the graph itself, it's writing contracts stable enough that a plugin written in year one still works in year five. agent.summary: Angular 20+ drops file suffixes like .component.ts, which breaks Ctrl+P habits such as typing ‘hoser’ for home.service.ts; Angular Suffix Lens reads each file and shows the suffixed name in VS Code without renaming anything on disk, and the broader point is that source code should be settled for the machine while tools project it however suits the human.
takeaways: Angular’s style guide and CLI no longer add .component/.service suffixes, so several files can share a name like home.ts.
Angular Suffix Lens detects the Angular type from file contents and shows the suffixed name in quick open, Explorer badges, a tree view and (optionally) tab titles.
Detection rules are regular expressions in settings, so teams can add their own kinds such as stores or facades.
Keep one minimal form of the source on disk and let tooling present it in whatever form fits the reader.

pages.text: Angular dropped the suffixes. I still wanted to type “hoser”. – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Writing / Angular dropped the suffixes. I still wanted to type “hoser”. Angular dropped the suffixes. I still wanted to type “hoser”. Angular no longer recommends .component.ts and .service.ts. A VS Code extension brings them back in the editor without renaming anything on disk. Published 2026-11-13 Angular Suffix Lens in action: Cmd+P, type “hoser”, open home.service.ts What changed For most of Angular’s history, the file name told you what was inside it: home.component.ts , home.service.ts , auth.guard.ts . Starting with Angular 20, the updated style guide dropped that recommendation, and the CLI dropped it too. When you run ng generate component home now, you get home.ts with a class named Home . A service gets the same treatment, so a new project can easily have two files that are both called home.ts . The reasoning makes sense. The suffix duplicates information that’s already in the code ( @Component , @Injectable ). It makes names longer, and it pushes people toward thinking in framework categories instead of naming things for what they do. On disk, I’m fine with it. My muscle memory isn’t. I’ve spent years opening files with Ctrl+P and a few letters: hoco for home.component.ts , hoser for home.service.ts . With suffix-less files, hoser finds nothing. If I type home instead, I get two identical-looking home.ts entries and have to read the folder path to tell which one I want. The file tree, the editor tabs and quick open all became a little harder to read. The extension: Angular Suffix Lens So I built Angular Suffix Lens . It reads each TypeScript file in your workspace, works out what kind of Angular thing it is, and shows the suffixed name throughout VS Code. Nothing is renamed on disk. Ctrl+P / Cmd+P: type hoser and home.service.ts comes up. It opens services/home.ts right at the decorator. Explorer badges: files get a small letter: C for component, S for service, D for directive, P for pipe, G for guard, and so on. Hovering over a badge shows the full Angular name. Companion files: home.html , home.css and home.spec.ts follow their component, so homecomhtml finds the template. Go to Angular File (Cmd+Alt+P / Ctrl+Alt+P): a picker ranked by Angular name. An “Angular Files” view that lists the whole project by its Angular names. Editor tab titles with the suffix (opt-in). Detection is driven by settings. Each rule is a regular expression plus a suffix and a badge, and the first match wins. The defaults cover components, directives, pipes, NgModules, guards, interceptors, resolvers and services, including the newer @Service() decorator. If your team has its own conventions (stores, facades, effects), you can add rules for them in settings.json . Setting the list replaces the defaults, so copy the default rules in first and then add your own: "angularSuffixes.rules" : [ { "suffix" : "store" , "pattern" : "signalStore \\ s* \\ (" , "badge" : "St" } , // ...followed by the default rules ] How it works VS Code doesn’t let extensions change how the built-in Ctrl+P matches file paths, and it doesn’t let them rename items in the Explorer. Both of those are deliberate, and they’re the right call. What it does allow: A workspace symbol provider . The extension registers every Angular file as a symbol named after its Angular name ( home.service.ts ). With search.quickOpen.includeSymbols turned on, those symbols show up in the normal Ctrl+P list, so hoser just works. The extension offers to turn that setting on for you. A file decoration provider for the Explorer badges and tooltips. VS Code’s custom editor labels setting, for tab titles. Indexing happens once on startup and is then kept current by a file watcher. It respects files.exclude and search.exclude , and it skips very large files. Try it code --install-extension ajwiebe.angular-suffix-lens Or search for “Angular Suffix Lens” in the Extensions view. The source is on GitHub at alexanderwiebe/angular-suffix-lens under the MIT license. Issues and pull requests are welcome, especially new detection rules. Closing thoughts: source code for the machine, views for the human The naming debate for Angular files always assumed there was one correct name, and that the file system was where it lived. One side wanted names that were short and honest. The other side wanted names that were easy to scan and search. Both are right, because they’re optimizing for different readers. The compiler, the bundler and git don’t care what a file is called. People reading a file tree or hunting for a file in quick open care a lot, and what they need changes with the task. When I’m navigating, I want home.service.ts . When I’m reading imports, home is plenty. A new team member might want every file labeled. Someone who has lived in the codebase for years might want nothing extra on screen at all. We already accept this split everywhere else. Syntax highlighting, inlay hints, code folding, git blame annotations and type-on-hover are all layers the editor draws over the source to help a person understand it, and none of them get saved into the file. File names have been the exception only because the file system is so literal. I think that’s the direction to keep pushing. Keep source code minimal and settle it for the machine: one canonical form, with no duplicated metadata and nothing extra to argue about in code review. Then let tooling project that source into whatever form makes the most sense to the person looking at it, on their screen and on their terms. The disk can say home.ts . My editor can say home.service.ts . Neither one has to be wrong. by AJ click to skip by AJ © AJ Wiebe source on github

outline.heading: The questions every post gets asked

for: Developers building sites for AI agents

agent.author_experience: Built the WebMCP layer for this site, including the post tools this post describes.

claims.claim: Agents answer questions about a post more reliably from structured tools than from scraped prose.

evidence.detail: Not yet measured; based on building this site’s tools.

claims.claim: Generating the tools from the post’s own frontmatter keeps the human and agent versions in sync.

evidence.detail: How this site builds every post.

limitations: WebMCP only works while the page is open in a browser that supports it, so crawlers and API-only agents don’t see the tools.

next_steps.action: Read how this site implements it

agent.summary: A blog post can serve human readers and AI agents at once: prose for people, and WebMCP tools built from the same file that answer the questions readers ask of any post.
takeaways: Readers ask the same ten questions of every post: what, for whom, by whom, what claim, what evidence, how good, how current, what bias, what context, what next.
Scholarly articles answer those questions in fixed sections. Blogs mostly don’t, so agents guess from the prose.
Typing each claim’s evidence (measured, experienced, cited, opinion) is the most useful single addition.

pages.text: Blog posts that answer agents back – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Writing / Blog posts that answer agents back Blog posts that answer agents back The post is for people. Its WebMCP tools are for the agents reading it on their behalf. Published 2026-11-04 Most blog posts are written to be read top to bottom by a person. More and more, they’re read by an agent on that person’s behalf, and the agent has to guess what the post claims and how sure the author is. The questions every post gets asked Is this for me? Who wrote it? How do they know? Is it current? Is it selling something? What do I do next? Scholarly articles answer these in required sections. Blogs mostly leave them implicit. How it works Each post’s frontmatter has an agent: block. The build turns it into WebMCP tools on the post’s page, one per question, while the reader sees only the post. What this doesn’t do It doesn’t verify anything. It gives an honest author a structured way to say what they know, how they know it, and where it stops applying. by AJ click to skip by AJ © AJ Wiebe source on github

pages.text: Asking this site questions with WebMCP – AJ Wiebe AJ WIEBE Software Engineer · Principal Consultant Light / Dark Writing Projects Research About Writing / Asking this site questions with WebMCP Asking this site questions with WebMCP Every page here registers tools an AI agent can call. Here’s what they are and what to ask. Published 2026-11-04 This site has two audiences: you, and whatever AI agent you bring with you. The pages are for you. For the agent, every page also registers WebMCP tools, small functions it can call to get answers as structured data instead of guessing from the layout. What you need A browser with WebMCP turned on and an agent that can use it. Chrome has it as an early preview; the Chrome for Developers docs explain how to enable it. Once a page loads, the tools are there. You don’t need to click or install anything on this site. No WebMCP browser? Skip to Without an agent . Site-wide questions These tools are registered on every page, so you can ask them from anywhere on the site. Ask something like Tool the agent should use “What is this site? What can I find here?” about_this_website “Who is AJ Wiebe and how do I contact him?” about_aj_wiebe “What’s on the page I’m looking at?” get_current_page “What pages are on this site? What does the Research page say?” list_pages , get_page “Where has AJ worked? What’s his education?” get_experience “What has AJ built?” list_projects “Tell me about the AI Briefing project.” get_project “What papers has AJ published? What’s he researching now?” list_research “What has AJ written?” list_posts “Give me the claims and evidence from the WebMCP post.” get_post “Search the site for knowledge graphs.” search_site “Switch to dark mode.” set_theme All of them only read, except set_theme , which changes the colour scheme and remembers your choice in this browser. get_post is worth knowing about. It returns a whole post’s thesis, audience, claims, sources and next steps without you opening it, so an agent can compare posts or decide which one is worth your time. Questions about one post Open a post and its page adds six more tools. They answer the questions people tend to ask of any article. Blog posts that answer agents back is a good one to try them on. Ask something like Tool the agent should use “Give me the one-line version.” / “Summarize this with its takeaways.” / “Outline it.” get_post_summary “I’m a platform engineer on a Hugo blog. Is this for me?” check_post_fit “What do I need to know before reading this?” check_post_fit “Why should I trust this? Is the author selling anything?” get_post_credibility “What does this claim, and what’s the evidence?” / “Which claims are only opinion?” get_post_claims “What does this build on? Does anything contradict it?” get_post_context “I’ve read it. What now? Where does this advice stop applying?” get_post_next_steps Every claim in a post is labelled with how the author knows it: measured (the author measured it), experienced (from the author’s own practice), cited (from a linked source) or opinion . Asking “which claims are only opinion?” is the quickest way to see how much a post rests on judgment. Good answers also say no when they should. Asking for a claim that doesn’t exist, or about a topic the post doesn’t cover, should come back as “not there”, not an invented answer. Without an agent The same tools are callable from page JavaScript in any browser. Open DevTools, go to the Console, and try: // Every tool registered on this page window . siteTools . list () . map (t => t . name ) // Call one; results are JSON strings JSON . parse ( await window . siteTools . call ( 'list_projects' , {})) JSON . parse ( await window . siteTools . call ( 'search_site' , { query : 'ontology' })) // On a post page JSON . parse ( await window . siteTools . call ( 'get_post_claims' , {})) Pass input as a plain object, not a JSON string. Bad input returns an error with the expected schema and an example rather than throwing. <html data-webmcp="..."> shows whether the browser accepted the tools: registered , partial , failed or unavailable . How it stays accurate The tools don’t keep a hand-written copy of the site. Each build writes an index of every rendered page, and the tools read that index or load the page itself, so when a page changes, the answers change with it. Post tools read the post’s agent: frontmatter, the same file the post itself is written in, so the prose and the structured answers can’t drift apart. The tools come from quarto-webmcp , a Quarto extension extracted from this site, so any Quarto site can do the same. What this doesn’t do The tools only exist while a page is open in a browser. A crawler or an API-only agent fetching the HTML won’t see them. And post answers are what the author wrote down: structure makes it easier to be honest about evidence, but it doesn’t check it. by AJ click to skip by AJ © AJ Wiebe source on github
